elements.element: Vendor may audit no more than once in any 12-month period.
elements.evidence: Rendered clause: "may, no more than once per year and upon no less than thirty (30) days prior written notice". The inserted cap limits inspections to one per annum; note "per year" is arguably calendar-year rather than any rolling 12-month period, a wording nuance only.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 30 days' written notice of an audit.
elements.evidence: Retained: "upon no less than thirty (30) days prior written notice to the Company".
Retained: "during the Company's normal business hours".

elements.element: Audits are conducted by an independent auditor.
elements.evidence: The inspection is performed by "HDI's General Manager" — a Vendor employee, not an independent auditor. No operative language substitutes an independent third-party auditor.

elements.element: The auditor is bound by confidentiality obligations.
elements.evidence: Section 3.4 as rendered contains no confidentiality undertaking applicable to the inspecting person; no such obligation was inserted.

elements.element: Audits are conducted off-site where possible.
elements.evidence: No location limitation appears; the clause contemplates inspection of Company records during Company business hours with no off-site preference language.

elements.element: Vendor bears audit costs unless underpayment exceeds 5 percent.
elements.evidence: Retained: "The fees incurred by HDI in connection with the inspection shall be borne by HDI." Cost sits unconditionally on Vendor, which is at least as favourable as the 5% carve-out.

elements.element: Vendor has no direct access to Customer systems for an audit.
elements.evidence: The clause grants a right to "inspect the records" but contains no express prohibition on direct access to Company systems; no such prohibition was added.

elements.element: Vendor may audit no more than once per year.
elements.evidence: Inserted operative text: "may, no more than once per year and upon no less than thirty (30) days prior written notice" — an express annual frequency cap replacing the previously unlimited right.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 15 days' notice of an audit.
elements.evidence: Already met by retained language: "no less than thirty (30) days prior written notice to the Company", exceeding the 15-day floor.

elements.element: Vendor bears audit costs unless underpayment exceeds 10 percent.
elements.evidence: Already met by retained language: "The fees incurred by HDI in connection with the inspection shall be borne by HDI" — Vendor bears cost in all cases, with no shift-back trigger at any threshold.

reasons: Fallback checklist is complete: the single inserted phrase supplies the missing annual frequency cap, while the retained 30-day notice and unconditional HDI-borne cost terms already meet or exceed the 15-day and 10%-underpayment fallback elements.

Preferred level remains incomplete on four elements — no independent auditor (the inspector is HDI's own General Manager), no confidentiality binding on the inspector, no off-site-where-possible preference, and no express bar on direct access to Company systems. To reach preferred the drafter would need operative text substituting an independent auditor bound by confidentiality, requiring off-site review where possible, and expressly excluding direct access to Company systems.

Minimality holds: the edit adds only "no more than once per year and" (plus necessary commas) and deletes nothing; the favourable 30-day notice, business-hours limit, records-scope limitation and Vendor-cost allocation are all retained verbatim, with no extras such as record-retention, remedies or survival tails.

Intent preserved: the payment-calculation verification mechanic, notice timing, business-hours anchor and cost allocation operate unchanged; no cross-reference, defined term (HDI's General Manager) or commercial mechanic is left dangling or contradicted.

Classification as a deviation is supportable: an unlimited inspection right fails the fallback frequency element on a material term and edges toward the walk-away 'unlimited audits' position, so a redline rather than a rationale-only note is appropriate.
